faqs.question: How many people count as a group Halloween costume?
faqs.answer: Four or more is the useful line, because three-person costumes are their own category with fixed casts. From four upward the question changes from 'who plays whom' to 'what still works if someone cancels', which is why this page sorts ideas by headcount.

faqs.question: What is a good Halloween costume for 4 people?
faqs.answer: The four seasons and the four elements are the classic fixed sets, and a condiment caddy of ketchup, mustard, mayo and relish is the cheapest. If one of the four might drop out, pick a crayon box or a deck of cards instead, since both still look complete with three.

faqs.question: What group costume works if we don't know how many people are coming?
faqs.answer: A crayon box, a deck of cards, an emoji set or a colour wheel. Nobody can tell how many crayons or cards a set should have, so a cancellation or a late joiner changes nothing in the photo.

faqs.question: How much does a group Halloween costume cost per person?
faqs.answer: By our build estimates, the scalable ideas run about $5–15 per person and the fixed-cast builds like the four seasons about $15–30. Setting a cap such as $20 per person before the vote keeps one expensive idea from winning.

faqs.question: How far ahead should a group choose its costume?
faqs.answer: Open a shared ideas doc about three weeks before 31 October and close the vote within 48 hours. That leaves two weeks for one person to bulk-buy fabric and face paint and for everyone to assemble their piece.

faqs.question: Which voting method works best for picking a group costume?
faqs.answer: Use an approval vote: everyone ticks every idea they would genuinely wear and the most ticks wins. It avoids the stalemate where each person votes only for their own idea, and a budget cap announced first removes the money argument.

faqs.question: What are easy last-minute group costumes?
faqs.answer: An emoji set needs only yellow tops, paper plates and a marker, and a ghost team needs only white sheets. Both take an hour or less per person and accept late joiners without any change to the theme.

faqs.question: What group costumes work for an office team?
faqs.answer: An out-of-office ghost team in white sheets over work clothes, or a colour wheel in department colours. Both are cheap, need no character knowledge and let anyone opt in on the day.

faqs.question: What are good group Halloween costumes for a family with kids?
faqs.answer: A pumpkin patch with kids as pumpkins and adults as the farmer and scarecrow works at any age. Keep the children's faces visible with face paint rather than full masks: a 1976 study of about 1,300 trick-or-treaters found more candy and money taken by anonymous children in groups.

faqs.question: Can our group share Halloween contact lenses?
faqs.answer: No. The FDA says decorative contact lenses need a prescription, should never be bought from a Halloween or novelty store and should never be shared with anyone else.

faqs.question: Can SubhSandesh make a group Halloween invitation or costume plan?
faqs.answer: No. The Halloween page is a one-person greeting with partner, bestie, family and kids modes; it does not collect votes or invite a crowd. It is useful for the one friend who missed the group photo.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Group Halloween Costumes Sorted by Size, From 4 to 10+ People

The best group Halloween costumes are the ones that still look finished when somebody drops out: a crayon box, a deck of cards, an emoji set or a colour wheel reads as complete at 4 people and at 14. On SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone, which is exactly where your group photo will be judged.

Groups also decide late: 49.4% of Raksha Bandhan pages on SubhSandesh were built on the festival day itself (n = 89, a different festival and a small sample; we hold no Halloween data). Below are ideas sorted by headcount (4, 5–6, 7–10, 10+, office and family), a decision table with hours, cost per person and dropout tolerance, and a plan for getting six people to agree before 31 October.

## What makes a group Halloween costume work?

A group Halloween costume is a set of outfits that reads as one idea only when the wearers stand together, so each piece can be simple as long as the set is legible. The practical test is a phone screen: if someone scrolling past your photo can name the theme in two seconds, it works.

Moving as a unit matters as much as matching. In a 2018 field experiment with 172 volunteers at Forsyth Barr Stadium in Dunedin, groups that marched in step and were physically aroused clustered more tightly and cooperated more in a free-rider game ([Jackson et al., Scientific Reports, 2018](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC5760525)). Arriving, posing and doing one rehearsed gesture together is the party-sized version.

What the costume signals also counts. In a 1979 lab study, people in nurse-style uniforms chose more prosocial options than people in robes resembling Ku Klux Klan garb; anonymity alone changed nothing, but it strengthened the effect of the friendly costume ([Johnson and Downing, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1979](https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2F0022-3514.37.9.1532)).

## 4 scalable group costumes that work for any headcount

These four are the safest halloween ideas for groups whose size is still moving. Each entry gives the same four facts in the same order: what it is, the group size it fits, cost and time per person (our estimates, not a survey), and what happens when someone cancels.

### 1. Crayon box

Everyone wears one solid colour head to toe, a paper cone hat in that colour and a black band with the colour's name hand-lettered on it. It fits 4 to 30 people at roughly $8–15 and 1–2 hours each, if people already own a plain top. Dropouts are invisible, because nobody at the party knows how many crayons the box was meant to hold.

### 2. Deck of cards

Each person wears two poster-board panels, front and back, painted as a different playing card. It fits 4 to 52 people at about $5–10 and an hour each, mostly lettering, and four people make a natural set of aces. Dropouts barely matter, since any number of cards is still a hand.

### 3. Emoji set

Yellow tops plus a hand-drawn face on a paper plate, worn as a mask or pinned to the chest, each person a different expression. It fits 4 to 20 people at $6–12 and 1–2 hours each. Losing one face goes unnoticed, and a late joiner only needs a plate and a marker, which makes this the strongest last-minute option on the page.

### 4. Colour wheel

Each person wears one hue, and you stand in rainbow order for the photo; the paint-swatch version adds a card with an invented paint name. It fits 6 to 24 people at $10–20 and about 2 hours each. A gap shows in a small wheel, so give red, yellow and blue to the three most reliable people.

## Group costume ideas by size: 4, 5–6, 7–10 and 10+

A fixed-cast idea breaks the moment one person cancels. Ideas marked "fixed" need exactly that number; everything else stretches.

### For 4 people

These cover most halloween ideas for 4 people, from five-minute to weekend builds:

- Four seasons: spring florals, summer sunglasses, autumn leaves, winter knitwear (fixed)
- Four elements: earth, water, fire and air in brown, blue, orange and white (fixed)
- Condiment caddy: ketchup, mustard, mayo and relish
- A garage band of drummer, bassist, guitarist and singer, with a band name you invent

### For 5–6 people

- Mystery-solving van gang: four amateur sleuths and their dog (fixed at 5)
- Five senses: a giant eye, ear, nose, mouth and hand worn as hats (fixed)
- Sushi platter: salmon nigiri, tamago, cucumber roll, wasabi and pickled ginger
- Full breakfast: eggs, bacon, toast, pancakes, coffee and orange juice
- A six-pack of identical soda cans, each labelled with an invented flavour

### For 7–10 people

- Days of the week, Monday in a dressing gown through Friday in party sequins (fixed at 7)
- The solar system: eight planets, with Pluto in a "still counts" sash and the Sun as a tenth
- A bowling lane: nine pins in white with red stripes, plus one person as the ball
- The seven dwarfs from the Grimm fairy tale, renamed after your group's own habits

### For 10+, office teams and families

- Office: an out-of-office ghost team, white sheets over work clothes with lanyards still on
- Office: the colour wheel in department colours, which settles who stands next to whom
- Family: a pumpkin patch, with kids as pumpkins and adults as the farmer and scarecrow
- Family: a gothic mansion household with a butler, a grandmother and a disembodied hand
- 15 or more: a full deck's court cards plus two jokers, or the solar system with moons

## How do you get 6 people to agree on a group costume?

Most group costumes die in the group chat. This five-step process costs each person about 20 minutes:

1. Open one shared doc about three weeks out (around 10 October). Everyone adds up to two ideas with a reference photo.
2. State the budget cap before anyone votes, for example $20 per person, so nobody champions a $60 inflatable.
3. Run an approval vote that closes in 48 hours: each person ticks every idea they would genuinely wear, and the most ticks wins.
4. Name one lead who buys in bulk: one fabric order, one tub of face paint, one roll of felt, split afterwards through a payment app.
5. Agree the dropout rule now: either pick a scalable idea or give the fixed roles understudies.

Do not expect anyone to start early without a deadline. In our nearest analogue, not one of 89 Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages was built more than 7 days ahead, and that was a solo task.

Running a group of kids? Keep their faces visible. In a 1976 Halloween field study of about 1,300 trick-or-treaters, concealed raters saw significantly more stealing of candy and money when children were anonymous and in a group, and the highest rates came from anonymous groups in which one child had been made responsible for the others ([Diener et al., Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1976](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1976-20842-001)). Face paint over full masks, name tags and an adult who is plainly in charge are the practical reading.

## Group Halloween costume decision table

The table compares five ideas on the four things that decide a group costume: how many people it fits, effort per person, cost per person and whether it survives a cancellation. Hours and dollar figures are our own build estimates, not survey data.

| Idea | Group size | Effort per person | Est. cost per person | Handles dropouts? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Crayon box | 4–30 | 1–2 hrs | $8–15 | Yes, fully |
| Deck of cards | 4–52 | 1 hr | $5–10 | Yes, fully |
| Emoji set | 4–20 | 1–2 hrs | $6–12 | Yes, and late joiners too |
| Four seasons | exactly 4 | 3–4 hrs | $15–30 | No, a missing season shows |
| Solar system | 8–10 | 4–6 hrs | $10–25 | Partly, drop the outer planets |

The takeaway: the three cheapest ideas are also the three that survive cancellations, so an unconfirmed group should pick from the top half. Fixed-cast ideas only make sense once every name is confirmed.

## When a group costume is the wrong call

A matching costume is the wrong choice when the group cannot commit a week out. In that case, agree only a shared colour or a shared prop and let everyone dress individually; the photo still reads as a set.

It is also wrong when budgets differ sharply. A $40 costume can be a hard no for one friend, and the cap in step 2 exists to stop that conversation happening at the till.

Matching cat-eye contact lenses are a bad group add-on. The [FDA's decorative contact lens guidance](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/contact-lenses/decorative-contact-lenses), updated 22 October 2024, says every decorative lens needs a prescription, should never be bought from a Halloween or novelty store, and should never be shared with anyone else.

SubhSandesh has a limit here too. Our [Halloween greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is a one-person page, not a group tool: it will not plan a costume, collect votes or invite a crowd. It is for the one friend who missed the photo.

You add their name, up to six photos (the group shot appears when they wipe fog off a portrait), a letter they read by flashlight, and bestie mode asks "Will you be my boo-st friend forever?" before it ends in a 1080×1920 Boo License. It takes about five minutes to make and is free to send.

If you want to add a voice note of up to 60 seconds or up to 12 photos, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) does that. It is still built for one recipient, and adds an optional unlock time and a one-message reply box.

## Sources

- Jackson, J. C. et al. (2018). [Synchrony and Physiological Arousal Increase Cohesion and Cooperation in Large Naturalistic Groups](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC5760525). Scientific Reports, 8, 127. Published 9 January 2018; open access, CC BY.
- Johnson, R. D. and Downing, L. L. (1979). [Deindividuation and valence of cues: Effects on prosocial and antisocial behavior](https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2F0022-3514.37.9.1532). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(9), 1532–1538. September 1979; abstract read, full text paywalled.
- Diener, E. et al. (1976). [Effects of deindividuation variables on stealing among Halloween trick-or-treaters](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1976-20842-001). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 33(2), 178–183. Abstract read, full text paywalled.
- U.S. Food and Drug Administration. [Decorative Contact Lenses for Halloween and More](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/contact-lenses/decorative-contact-lenses). Content current as of 22 October 2024.

sources.stat: Field experiment, 172 participants, Forsyth-Barr Stadium, Dunedin: synchrony and arousal each predicted larger groups, tighter clustering and more cooperation in a free-rider dilemma; synchrony tightened clustering and raised cooperation only when paired with arousal. Full text read (Europe PMC, CC BY).

Johnson & Downing 1979, JPSP 37(9):1532–1538: costume cue (nurse uniform vs Klan-like robe) had a main effect on shock choices; no main effect of deindividuation; deindividuation significantly increased prosocial responses with positive cues. Abstract only read; full text paywalled.

Diener, Fraser, Beaman & Kelem 1976, JPSP 33(2):178–183: ~1,300 trick-or-treating children observed by concealed raters; significantly more stealing of candy and money under anonymity and in groups; highest rates among anonymous children in groups with altered responsibility. Abstract only read; full text paywalled (closed access per OpenAlex).

All decorative lenses must be prescribed; never buy from a Halloween or novelty store; 'Don't share your contact lenses with anyone else!' Content current as of 10/22/2024 (dateModified, no publication date).

batchMeta.siblingSplit: Groups of 4+ only. Duos -> halloween-costumes-for-best-friends; exactly 3 -> trio-halloween-costumes; party decor themes -> halloween-party-themes; brand/office marketing -> halloween-marketing-ideas. No /blog/ links.
structuralLimitations: Brief said the Diener 1976 study is about 'children taking extra candy'. The APA abstract says concealed raters observed ~1,300 trick-or-treaters given the chance to steal candy AND money; stealing rose with anonymity and group presence, highest among anonymous groups where one child was made responsible. The paper is closed access (OpenAlex: closed, no repository copy), so only the abstract was read and the body says so.
Johnson & Downing 1979 found NO main effect of deindividuation; the effect was the costume cue. The body states this rather than the popular 'masks make people bad' reading.
Cost-per-person and effort-hour figures are our own build estimates, labelled in the body: nrf.com is capped, and no non-competitor source prices group costumes.
No Halloween first-party data exists; the lead-time figures are Raksha Bandhan (n = 89), disclosed in body prose at both uses.
Search budget: 2 Firecrawl searches used (SERP + one to locate the Johnson & Downing record). The 'halloween ideas for 4 people' variant SERP was not measured separately.
nature.com returned a bot challenge; the Jackson et al. paper was read in full via the Europe PMC full-text XML instead.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a reason to cite this over the five pages analysed: it is the only one that sorts by headcount with cost, hours and dropout tolerance, explains how a group decides, and accurately reports the Diener trick-or-treat and Johnson & Downing costume-cue findings. The first-party data is analogue rather than costume data, and the SERP is dominated by Good Housekeeping, Teen Vogue and costume retailers with far more authority and image libraries, so this page competes on the coordination and decision-table sub-queries, not the image-led head term.
